front: {{c1::Groupthink}} occurs when a cohesive group's desire for consensus suppresses dissent and realistic appraisal, producing bad decisions.
why: Groupthink is named on 7B and tested on essentially every administration

front: {{c1::Role conflict}} is tension between roles of two different statuses; {{c2::role strain}} is tension among expectations within a single role.
why: Role conflict vs role strain is tested on essentially every administration

front: {{c1::Role exit}} is disengaging from a central role and rebuilding identity — retiring, leaving a religious order, divorcing.
why: Role exit is named on the 8C outline; appears as a discrete

front: {{c1::Social loafing}} is reduced individual effort in groups when contributions are unidentifiable, e.g., slacking in a group project.
why: Social loafing is named on 7B and tested every year

front: {{c1::Transactional}} leadership exchanges rewards for performance; {{c2::transformational}} leadership motivates through vision and inspiration.
why: Transactional/transformational leadership not on AAMC outline

front: A {{c1::dyad}} (Simmel) is the most intimate, least stable group; adding a member creates a {{c2::triad}}, allowing mediation and coalitions.
why: Simmel dyad/triad stability is a common group-size discrete

front: A {{c1::master status}} overrides all others in how one is perceived — 'ex-convict', 'blind', 'celebrity', often 'physician'.
why: Master status is foundational 8C status vocabulary tested every year

front: A {{c1::primary}} group (Cooley) has intimate, enduring bonds valued in themselves (family); a {{c2::secondary}} group is impersonal and goal-directed.
why: Primary vs secondary group is core 8C, tested every administration

front: A {{c1::reference}} group supplies the standards we use to evaluate ourselves, e.g., a premed measuring against admitted medical students.
why: Reference group is core 8C and underlies relative deprivation questions

front: A hospital committee arrives at a more extreme decision than any member held alone. Name the phenomenon and both directions it can take.
why: Group polarization applied; risky vs cautious shift is commonly tested

front: A nurse must work the night of her daughter's recital, and also feels torn between speed and thoroughness on shift. Label each tension.
why: Role conflict/strain is tested as an applied scenario exactly like this

front: An {{c1::ascribed}} status is assigned involuntarily (race, sex, birth cohort); an {{c2::achieved}} status is earned (physician, felon, spouse).
why: Ascribed vs achieved status is foundational 8C, tested every year

front: An {{c1::in-group}} commands loyalty and a sense of 'we'; an {{c2::out-group}} is 'they', often viewed with competition or contempt.
why: In-group/out-group is core 8C and drives bias questions every year

front: Compare authoritarian, democratic, and laissez-faire leadership styles.
why: Leadership styles are off-outline prep content; skippable

front: Compare the central and peripheral routes to persuasion.
why: Central vs peripheral route (ELM) is tested on essentially every exam

front: Contrast Gemeinschaft and Gesellschaft (Tonnies).
why: Tonnies is off-outline; useful parallel to primary/secondary groups

front: Contrast groupthink and group polarization.
why: Discriminating groupthink from polarization is the way both get tested

front: Contrast instrumental and expressive leadership.
why: Instrumental/expressive leadership not on AAMC outline

front: Describe cognitive dissonance and its resolution.
why: Cognitive dissonance is tested every year as discrete or passage step

front: Distinguish a group from an aggregate and a category.
why: Group vs aggregate vs category is a common discrete definition item

front: Explain the bystander effect.
why: Bystander effect is named on 7B and tested every administration

front: How can a secondary group become a primary group?
why: Elaboration of the primary/secondary group card (13)

front: In hospital codes, the most effective fix for delayed action is assigning each task to a named person. Which two group processes does that counteract?
why: Applied diffusion of responsibility/social loafing; scenario-style testing

front: In Milgram's studies, obedience DECREASED when:
why: Milgram variations (proximity, authority distance) are frequently tested

front: Name the concrete structural remedies Janis proposed to prevent groupthink.
why: Janis's specific remedy list is detail beyond the groupthink concept

front: Social loafing is:
why: Restates social loafing card (9)

front: What did Asch and Milgram each demonstrate?
why: Asch conformity and Milgram obedience are tested every administration

front: What is a role set (Merton)?
why: Merton role set is secondary status/role vocabulary

front: What is group polarization?
why: Group polarization is named on 7B and tested every year

front: What is social facilitation?
why: Social facilitation is named on 7B and tested every year

front: What is the relationship between status and role?
why: Status vs role is the foundational 8C distinction, tested every year

front: Why did Simmel consider triads more stable than dyads, despite dyads' greater intimacy?
why: Restates the dyad/triad card (11)
